title: The night of the senses
hook: when prayer stops feeling good, God may be weaning us from the sweets

segments.voice: Yesterday, the dark night: a love poem, a sleeping house, a soul slipping out to meet God. Your line was my house being now at rest. Today, John explains the first part of that night.

People who pray don't always say this out loud. At the start, it can feel wonderful. Mass, a quiet church, a psalm read slowly, and something warm comes. Tears, sometimes. Peace. Going back is easy. Then one day it's just gone. Show up, say the words. Nothing. Flat as cardboard. It's easy to conclude that something went wrong, or that God has left, or that it was never real. John of the Cross had a very different explanation.
screen: `AT FIRST, IT FEELS WONDERFUL.` → `THEN ONE DAY, NOTHING.` → `DID GOD LEAVE?`

segments.voice: First, the mother. John opens his book the Dark Night with a homely picture. A loving mother holds her baby close, warms it, and feeds it sweet milk. That's how God treats beginners in prayer, he says: with comfort and sweetness. Second, the weaning. But a mother who loves her child doesn't nurse it forever. One day she weans it. She sets it down so it will learn to walk, and it cries for the milk. Saint Paul says something similar to one young church, in the Douay-Rheims: "I gave you milk to drink, not meat; for you were not able as yet." John says God does the same with souls. The sweetness is taken away, not to punish, but so they can grow. Third, the sweet tooth. John is funny and sharp about beginners. He lists their faults in prayer: wanting more and more good feelings, a spiritual sweet tooth; judging others who seem less devout; sulking when prayer is dull. The night of the senses is God's cure for all that. When the feelings dry up, you find out whether you were seeking God, or the sweets God gave. Fourth, dry is not gone. Dryness in prayer, John says, can be a sign that God is closer, not farther, doing the work quietly, below what you can feel. He doesn't say every dry spell is this; tomorrow he gives ways to tell. But he says: don't assume God left because the sweetness did.
screen: `A MOTHER FEEDS HER BABY MILK.` · `THEN SHE WEANS IT TO WALK.` · `A SPIRITUAL SWEET TOOTH.` · `DRY IS NOT GONE.` · then, large: `I GAVE YOU MILK TO DRINK, NOT MEAT.`

segments.voice: Pray even if it's dry: sit, breathe, and don't try to make anything happen. If you pray, just be with God, even if it feels like talking to a wall; that counts. If you don't, sit with something you've been faithful to that doesn't feel exciting anymore, a friendship, a job, a promise, and notice that showing up still matters.
Sweetness. The comfort God gives beginners in prayer, which the night of the senses takes away, the way a mother weans a child, so the soul can grow. Today's word.
Your line: dry is not gone. A mother weans the child she loves. Two hundred sixty-one days in.

howItsDone: Catholic spiritual directors often turn to John's Dark Night, book one, when people say prayer has gone dry, and encourage them to keep praying faithfully rather than chasing feelings.

chat.says: Prayer used to feel warm, and now it feels flat. Did God leave me?
options: John would say not necessarily; dryness can mean God is closer, working below feelings.
John would say yes; when the warm feelings go, God has gone with them.
John would say it means you did something wrong and must track it down.
chat.meaning: John says God weans beginners from sweetness so they can grow. Dry is not gone; God may be working quietly below what you feel.

notes: The nursing mother who weans her child (Dark Night 1.1.2) and the beginners' imperfections under the seven capital sins, including 'spiritual gluttony' (1.2–7), paraphrased. 'Spiritual sweet tooth' is our gloss on spiritual gluttony. Confirm.
1 Corinthians 3:2 is offered as a parallel; John does cite Paul's milk and solid food image in his works, but confirm whether in this chapter.
The script notes that not every dry spell is the dark night, pointing to tomorrow's three signs.
